text:
You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance. But keep some room to explore life on your own.

For me, that room is where I keep a mission of my own, separate interests and some connection to community. I also get outside therapy when I need it, and I make sure I can still be alone.
section: Don’t make your partner your whole world
reader: someone reading an essay on romance for advice they can use in their own dating and relationships

sentences.s: You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance.
sentences.payoff: they know they can see friends less than before the romance without guilt.
sentences.follows: it opens the section on an allowance, and what it follows from depends on the friends paragraphs before it.
sentences.link: none: first sentence after heading, with nothing in it tying it to the heading

sentences.s: But keep some room to explore life on your own.
sentences.payoff: they keep some time and space for themselves instead of giving it all to the partner.
sentences.follows: it turns S1's allowance into the limit.

sentences.s: For me, that room is where I keep a mission of my own, separate interests and some connection to community.
sentences.payoff: they see what the room can hold by looking at the author's own list.
sentences.follows: it says what the room in S2 is for.

sentences.s: I also get outside therapy when I need it, and I make sure I can still be alone.
sentences.payoff: they know outside therapy and being able to be alone are also part of keeping a life apart.
sentences.follows: it adds two more items to S3's list.

placement: It depends on the two paragraphs before it about friends, which are not in the text; it fits the heading once S2 says to keep some room.

questions.Q1: PASS: S1 gives a point at once, though only S2 connects it to the heading.
questions.Q2: PASS: 'keep some room to explore life on your own' says its purpose.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
